blocks.text: that is, many of which are black in colour. Yet one serpent is black above the rest, and for that very reason it is called in Arabic اسود [aswad] asuad, that is, black. Alcamus: الاسود الحية العظيمة [al-aswad al-ḥayya al-ʿaẓīma] Alasuad (the black one), a great serpent ^{(4)}. Some add سالخ [sālikh] salich as an epithet, as if you were to say one coming out [III, 153], which Damir explains thus: الاسود السالخ نوع من الحيات شديد السواد سمي بذلك لانه يسلخ جلده كل عام [al-aswad al-sālikh nawʿ min al-ḥayyāt shadīd al-sawād summiya bi-dhālika li-annahu yaslukhu jildahu kull ʿām] Alasuad assalich, a kind of serpent of the most intense blackness, which is so called because it sheds its skin every year. Another copy has نوع من الافعوان [nawʿ min al-afʿuwān] a kind of viper. I understand black asps, which many Arabs include under the kind of vipers. These asps are indeed very black, as besides Nicander is taught by Pausanias, Aelian, Aëtius, and some of the Arabs. Granted this, the ancients rightly interpret שחל sachal as asp. Damir tells many fables about the black serpent, which I am loath to relate here. Among them: that Jesus, son of Mary, foretold to a woodcutter that on that very day he would fall into the gravest danger to his life. When he had gone to cut wood and returned towards evening with a bundle of wood, and at Christ's command had untied it, he found in it حية سودا [ḥayya sūdā] a black serpent. Then, when Jesus asked what he had done, and he denied having done anything except that he had given part of his bread to a passing beggar, Jesus replied: بهذا دفع عنك [bi-hādhā dafaʿa ʿanka] For this reason God has turned evil away from you. Others tell the same of [col. 379] Saleh, the prophet, and say that the serpent اسود سالخ [aswad sālikh] asuad salich was as thick مثل الجذع [mithl al-jidhʿ] as the trunk of a palm.
